items.title: *Design*
items.intro: A plan for the whole garden, drawn to scale.
items.description: Garden design by Tollgarth: a survey, a concept, a scaled plan and a planting plan for gardens in south-west London and Surrey.

photo.alt: A formal parterre garden seen from above

items.body:
We start in your garden: how you use it, where the sun falls, what stays. Then a survey, two or three ideas on paper, and one plan drawn to scale.

The planting plan names every plant and where it goes. You can stop at the drawings and use your own builder, or we build it.

items.title: *Build*
items.intro: Our own team, from the first level to the last plant.
items.description: Garden building by Tollgarth: paving, walls, decking, drainage and planting by one team in south-west London and Surrey.

photo.alt: Herringbone brick paving in low sun

items.body:
One team builds the garden: levels and drainage, walls and paving, then the planting. The person who drew it visits every week.

We protect the house and the way through it, and leave the site swept each evening.

points.label: How long
points.value: Usually four to ten weeks on site, said in the quote.

points.label: Payments
points.value: A deposit to book, then stages as the work is done.

points.label: Guarantee
points.value: New planting replaced once in its first year if it fails.

items.title: *Care*
items.intro: So the garden grows the way it was drawn.
items.description: Garden care by Tollgarth: maintenance visits through the year for gardens we've made and ones we haven't.

photo.alt: An avenue of clipped yew cones

items.body:
A new garden takes two or three years to fill in. Care visits keep it on course: pruning at the right time, feeding, replacing what didn't take.

We look after gardens we didn't make too, after a first visit.

gardenPages.title: Gardens
gardenPages.intro: Courtyards, roof terraces, family and country gardens.

items.title: A stone terrace in Barnes
items.description: A south-west garden in Barnes: a pale granite terrace by the house, white walls and wide steps up to a lawn.
items.brief: Somewhere to eat outside, and a lawn the children can have.
items.body:
The garden rose towards the back. We cut a level terrace by the house in pale granite, rendered the retaining walls white so they hold the evening light, and set wide steps up to the lawn.

Clipped standards and low hedges hold the edges; the cedar boards above the walls will silver in a year or two.

items.title: A town garden in Fulham
items.description: A south-facing town garden in Fulham: a clipped box hedge, roses against old brick and a path to the door.
items.brief: A garden that looks good from the kitchen in January.
items.body:
The house is late Victorian, so we kept to its brick and stone. A box hedge gives the garden its shape in winter; roses and climbers fill it from May.

The path was relaid in reclaimed stone on its old line, and a stone urn marks the turn to the door.

items.title: A walled garden in Islington
items.description: A north-facing walled garden in Islington: reclaimed brick, climbing roses and shade planting.
items.brief: A shaded yard that feels like a room.
items.body: Four walls and very little sun. We laid reclaimed brick to match the house, trained roses up the one wall that gets the afternoon, and planted the rest for shade.

items.title: A roof garden in Clerkenwell
items.description: A south-facing roof garden in Clerkenwell: oak decking, wind-proof planting and a view.
items.brief: Green all year, and still standing after a winter gale.
items.body: Every plant was chosen for wind and sun. The deck is air-dried oak, left to silver; the planters sit on the structure's own beams.

items.title: *Courtyards*
items.description: Courtyard gardens by Tollgarth: small, walled and shaded spaces in London made into rooms.

photo.alt: A white garden wall with climbing roses, two chairs on gravel

items.body:
A courtyard is a room without a roof. Walls give shelter and shade; every surface is seen from the house.

We plan for the light it has, choose one material for the floor, and plant up the walls.

items.title: *Roof* terraces
items.description: Roof terraces by Tollgarth: planting chosen for wind and sun, decking and planters built to the roof's limits.

photo.alt: A roof garden with curved planting beds and paving, city buildings beyond

items.body:
Roofs are windy, hot and dry. We work to the structural engineer's loads, choose plants that take wind, and water automatically.

The planting is for every season, because a roof is seen from inside all winter.

items.title: Country *gardens*
items.description: Country gardens by Tollgarth: meadows, avenues and long borders in Surrey.

photo.alt: A meadow planting in soft summer light

items.body:
In a large garden the plan matters more than any single plant: where the paths go, what you see from the house, where the garden meets the fields.

We plant for the long view, and phase the work over years if that suits.

items.title: What to plant in November
items.summary: Bare-root hedges, trees and the last of the tulips: why November is the best month to plant.

photo.alt: Copper beech leaves turned brown in autumn

items.body:
The soil is still warm from summer and the rain has come back. Roots grow on through the winter, so a hedge planted now is ahead of one planted in spring.

Bare-root plants come from the nursery without pots, from November to March. They are cheaper, and they settle quicker.

Tulips can go in until the end of the month. Plant them deep, three times their own height.

items.title: Designing a small garden
items.summary: In a small garden every surface is seen from the house. Four things we do first.

photo.alt: A walled courtyard with stone benches and a pool

items.body:
Choose one material for the floor and use it everywhere. Mixed paving makes a small space look smaller.

Plant up the walls. Climbers and wall shrubs give green without taking floor.

Build seats into the walls. Furniture that stays out all year saves space.

Light it. A small garden lit at night becomes part of the room it faces.

planning.title: Do I need *permission*?
planning.intro: Fences, decking, garden rooms and front gardens, in plain words.

rows.q: A new fence, wall or gate
rows.a: Usually not, up to 2 metres high. Next to a road used by vehicles, or its footpath, the limit is 1 metre. Not around a listed building.
Usually not, if it is no more than 30 centimetres above the ground. Higher than that counts as a raised platform and needs permission.

rows.q: A garden room, studio or shed
rows.a: Usually not, if it is single storey, behind the front of the house, and no more than 2.5 metres high within 2 metres of a boundary (otherwise 4 metres with a pitched roof, 3 metres with any other). It can't be a bedroom, and buildings and extensions together can't cover more than half the garden.
Over 5 square metres, the paving must let water through, or drain to a lawn or border. Otherwise it needs permission.

questions.q: Do you design, build, or both?
questions.a: Both. You can have the design alone and use your own builder, or we build it with our own team.
Usually six weeks to design, then a build slot about eight weeks later, and four to ten weeks on site.
A fixed fee for each design stage, quoted after the first visit. The build is quoted from the final drawings.
Yes. We draw all year and build whenever the ground can be worked. Many plants go in best between November and March.

questions.q: We have no side access. Will you go through the house?
questions.a: Only if there's no other way, with the floors and walls covered. We'll talk it through at the first visit.

questions.q: Do you look after gardens you didn't make?
questions.a: Yes, after a first visit to see it.
